title: The Discovery of Gobekli Tepe

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Near an ancient city in south eastern Turkey, archaeologist Klaus Schmidt has made a startling discovery: massive carved stones, crafted by prehistoric people. The place is called Gobekli Tepe. Schmidt has surveyed the main excavation site where the standing stones, or pillars, are arranged in circles. Beyond, on the hillside, are four other rings of partially excavated pillars. Each ring has a similar layout: in the centre are two large stone T-shaped pillars encircled by smaller stones facing inward. The tallest pillars tower 16 feet and weigh approximately ten tons.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: From 1,000 feet above the valley, Schmidt can easily imagine the landscape before centuries of intensive farming and settlement turned it into the nearly featureless brown expanse it is today. Prehistoric people would have gazed upon herds of gazelle, gently flowing rivers, migrating geese, and fields of wild wheat. 'This area was like a paradise,' says Schmidt.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: He explains he has mapped the entire summit using ground-penetrating radar and geomagnetic surveys, charting where at least 16 other megalith rings remain buried across 22 acres. In fact, Gobekli Tepe was first examined – and dismissed – by University of Chicago and Istanbul University anthropologists in the 1960s. They assumed the small hill was nothing more than a medieval cemetery. In 1994, after reading their report, Schmidt decided to go himself. From the moment he saw it, he knew the place was extraordinary. Gobekli Tepe has a gently rounded top that rises 50 feet above the landscape. To Schmidt's eye, the shape stood out. 'Only man could have created something like this,' he says.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Schmidt returned with five colleagues to excavate the 11,000-year-old site and they uncovered the first megaliths. However, they found none of the telltale signs of a settlement: no cooking hearths or trash pits. The archaeologists did find evidence of tool use, including hammers made of stone. Because those artefacts resemble others from nearby sites previously carbon-dated to about 9000 B.C., Schmidt estimates Gobekli Tepe's stone structures are the same age. Even without metal chisels or hammers, prehistoric masons using flint tools could have chipped away at limestone, since it is soft enough to shape into pillars, before carrying these a few hundred yards to the summit. Then, Schmidt says, once the stone rings were finished, the ancient builders covered them over with dirt. Eventually, they placed another ring nearby or on top of the old one. Over centuries, these layers created the hilltop.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Today, Schmidt oversees a large team that excavates the site for two months in the spring and two in the fall. Summer temperatures reach 115 degrees Fahrenheit, too hot to dig; in the winter the area is deluged by rain. Joris Peters, an archaeozoologist, has found clear evidence that animals in the region were butchered and cooked. 'The first year, we went through 15,000 animal bones, all of them wild. It was pretty clear we were dealing with a hunter-gatherer site,' Peters says. All this indicates that the people who lived here had not yet domesticated animals or farmed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Schmidt says Gobekli Tepe's builders were on the verge of a major change in how they lived, thanks to an environment that held the raw materials for farming. 'They had wild sheep, wild grains that could be domesticated – and the people with the potential to do it,' Schmidt says. To him and others, these new findings suggest a novel theory of civilization. Scholars have long believed that only after people learned to farm and live in settled communities did they have the time and resources to construct temples and support complicated social structures. But Schmidt argues that it was the other way around: the coordinated effort to build the megaliths facilitated the development of complex societies. Schmidt says carving rings of seven-ton stone pillars would have required hundreds of workers, all needing to be fed and housed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What was so important to these early people that they gathered to build the stone rings? There are no sources to explain what the symbols might mean. Gary Rollefson, an archaeologist at Whitman College, Washington, who is familiar with Schmidt's work, says: 'Trying to pick out the symbolism from a prehistoric context is an exercise in futility.' Still, archaeologists have their theories. The surprising lack of evidence that people lived right there, researchers say, argues against its use as a settlement. Stanford University archaeologist Ian Hodder is fascinated that Gobekli Tepe's pillar carvings are dominated not by edible prey like deer and cattle, but by creatures such as lions, scorpions and vultures. 'It's a scary, fantastic world of nasty-looking beasts,' he muses. While later cultures were more concerned with farming and fertility, he suggests perhaps these hunters were trying to master their anxieties by building this complex.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Danielle Stordeur, an archaeologist from France, emphasizes the significance of the vulture carvings. Some cultures believed these birds transported the flesh of the dead up to the heavens. Stordeur has found similar symbols at sites from the same era as Gobekli Tepe just 50 miles away. 'You can really see it's the same culture,' she says. 'All the most important symbols are the same.' As for Schmidt, he has also found fragments of human bone. Perhaps, he says, the site was a burial ground. If so, Gobekli Tepe's location was no accident. 'From here the dead are looking out at the ideal view,' Schmidt says. 'They're looking out over a hunter's dream.'

groups.title: Evidence and theories about the purpose of Gobekli Tepe
content: Gobekli Tepe is estimated to have been built around 11,000 years ago. As no household objects have been found at the excavation, it seems clear it was not a place of {{23}} for prehistoric people. Archaeologists have found tools like {{24}} . In fact, even without sophisticated tools, the pillars that form the rings would have been possible to carve because they were made of {{25}} , which isn't very hard.

Evidence that the builders of Gobekli Tepe were hunter-gatherers has been obtained by looking at {{26}} from animals found there. Finally, the fact that vultures have been carved onto the pillars suggests that Gobekli Tepe may have been used as a burial ground.
